title: Flu Hospitalizations Jump 38% in a Week as Texas Launches New Respiratory Virus Dashboard
excerpt: U.S. flu hospital admissions rose 38% in one week to 8,396, the CDC reported, and Texas has launched a new dashboard tracking flu, COVID-19 and RSV across the state.
content:
Flu hospital admissions across the United States jumped 38% in a single week, rising to 8,396 in the week ending Oct. 31, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention's latest FluView report — and Texas has launched a new tool to help residents track the viruses circulating here.

The CDC's Week 43 FluView report, published Nov. 6, found that 9.1% of specimens tested by clinical laboratories were positive for influenza, and almost all positives were influenza A. The agency estimates at least 1.7 million illnesses, 25,000 hospitalizations and 1,400 deaths from flu so far this season, up from 1 million illnesses, 16,000 hospitalizations and 900 deaths a week earlier. Three pediatric flu deaths have been reported this season.

The CDC's FluSight forecasting program predicts admissions will likely keep rising nationally through the week ending Nov. 21 — the week before Thanksgiving — with a forecast range of 6,900 to 30,100 new admissions that week. The CDC cautioned that an earlier rise in activity does not necessarily mean a higher peak or a more severe season overall.

Flu activity is higher than usual for this time of year, and most viruses detected so far are influenza A(H1N1)pdm09, according to the CDC. The next FluView report, covering the week ending Nov. 7, is due today.

Texas launches a new dashboard

The Texas Department of State Health Services has launched a new respiratory virus dashboard, accessible through DSHS's Texas Health Data site, showing trends in illness from influenza, COVID-19 and RSV — the three respiratory viruses most likely to cause serious disease at this time of year. The dashboard includes emergency room visits, hospitalizations and deaths.

"Those data points demonstrate the diseases' most severe effects on people, communities and the health care system," said DSHS Commissioner Jennifer Shuford, MD, MPH. "The dashboard provides a near real-time look at conditions, so people can make informed decisions on precautions for themselves and their families, and health care professionals can make recommendations to their patients."

DSHS is also publishing a new weekly respiratory virus surveillance report, combining separate reports on influenza, COVID-19 and RSV. The report includes information on the burden of influenza-like illness, counties where different types of flu have been found, and the proportions of COVID-19 variants present in Texas.

Respiratory virus season runs from October to May and usually peaks in the winter, DSHS said. In its earlier state-by-state data, Texas recorded respiratory illness visits at about 3% of outpatient visits — above the national figure, according to Becker's Hospital Review.

DSHS notes that getting immunized against respiratory viruses is a good way to protect against the severe disease, hospitalization and death they can cause, and that people can also help slow the spread by washing hands frequently with soap and water, covering coughs and sneezes, and staying home when sick.

All CDC figures cited here are preliminary and may change as more reports arrive.
